note: Levels 1 to 7. Every rule the game checks is data in this file, so an instructor or a reviewer can read it without reading code.

window.note: About 3 years of daily returns, over each portfolio's own overlapping days, as docs/PRD.md asks for a single portfolio. The daily 'Same bet?' puzzle uses one year instead, by its own design. Level 6 does not use this window: it carries its own, a fixed stretch of 2020 that never moves.
window.appliesTo: Every level whose prices come from data/game.json, which is levels 1 to 5 and 7. Level 6 carries its own window, a fixed stretch of 2020.

stressTest.note: The stress scenario Sandbox and My real portfolio show, and the days the second beta is measured on. docs/PRD.md defines the loss as 'portfolio value x beta x shock size' and the days as 'worst 10% of daily S&P 500 returns in the window', but it fixes no shock size, so the size is fixed here - before any portfolio was ever measured with it - rather than in code.
stressTest.shockNote: A round 20% fall in the AI basket. Round and memorable, chosen for being a plain number rather than for the loss it produces, and it does not move when data/game.json is refreshed - so a player who comes back to the same portfolio next week reads the same scenario. The RANGE on the screen comes from the two betas, all days and stress days, which is the instability docs/PRD.md says the range is there to show; a shock that moved with the data would mix a second kind of movement into it.

stressDays.note: The worst 10% of the S&P 500's days in the SAME window every other measure uses - the 756 above, not however many rows data/game.json happens to keep - which comes to 75 days. A count, not a percentile: floor(days x fraction), ranked by return, ties broken by date, so the set is the same set every time and a numpy fixture can name it exactly. The benchmark is the index rather than the AI basket, as docs/PRD.md requires, so that stress is not defined by the stocks under study.

kinds.note: What counts as a stock, for level 6's rule that at least 60% of the money sits in stocks. A stock fund is a stock: VOO, QQQ and VXUS are shares bought in one line. BND, TLT and LQD are loans, and GLD is metal, so none of the four is.
kinds.coverNote: 36 + 4, which is exactly tickers.json's 40 playable tickers. Both lists are written out rather than only the four exceptions: with an exceptions list, a bond fund added later would count as a stock in silence. tests/levels.test.js holds the union to the ticker list and the two lists to being disjoint, so a new ticker fails the test until it is classified here.
kinds.pltrNote: PLTR is a stock and is listed as one. It cannot be held in level 6 for a different reason - it had not listed in February 2020 - and mixing the two reasons would be a way to get the wrong answer later.

levels.title: Two of a kind
levels.challenge: Pick two holdings with different names that move together.
levels.hint: Two funds that hold almost the same companies move almost as one, whatever their names are. Look for a pair from the same heading rather than two names you recognise.
levels.poolNote: Fourteen names with several same-bet pairs in them, and a near miss that matters: VTI and VXUS correlate at 0.7997 over the current window, a hair under the threshold. It is shown to 4 decimals so the number on screen cannot read as a pass.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: how closely do these two move together, from -1 to 1?

levels.bucketNote: The same three buckets the daily 'Same bet?' puzzle uses.
levels.explain: Two holdings with different names can be the same bet. Correlation measures how closely their daily moves line up: 1 means they move together every day, 0 means their moves are unrelated.
levels.why: An S&P 500 fund and a total-market fund hold almost the same companies in almost the same proportions, so they rise and fall together. The names differ; the bet does not.

share.headline: I found two holdings with a correlation of {value}. Can you beat it?

levels.revealPlacesNote: A correlation is revealed to THREE decimals, not the two every other level uses. Two is not enough here: a real 0.9962 reads as "1.00", which claims a pair that moves together perfectly and is a claim the card then posts. Three reads 0.996. This is the revealed answer only - guess.places still describes the slider, which moves in hundredths - and js/round.js formats the panel, the result line, the "Why?" card and the share card through it together, so no two of them can disagree about the same pair.
levels.revealLabel: How closely they really move together

levels.title: How many bets?
levels.challenge: Here is a starter portfolio. Guess how many separate bets it really makes, then see the answer.
levels.hint: This level cannot be failed - its pass condition is "make a guess" - so the hint has no way of appearing. It is written down so that every level has one and a reader is not left wondering which is missing.
levels.hintNote: Unreachable by design - see hint. Every other level's hint is shown on the build screen once that level has been finished three times without earning a star.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: how many separate bets does this portfolio make?
guess.rangeNote: 1 to 6, the same slider level 7 uses. Hypothesis 3 compares a player's level-2 guess error with their level-7 error, so the two guesses have to be typed on the same instrument: a different midpoint, or a different distance per drag, could shift a guess for a reason that has nothing to do with learning. Changed before any player data existed. See BUILD_LOG.md, session 2.10.

levels.explain: Effective bets counts independent sources of risk, not holdings: five that move together are closer to one bet. It measures risk, not money: a bond fund can hold much of the money yet add little to the count.
levels.why: Drawn from a pool of 20 that level 7 also uses, so the two are equally hard on average.

share.headline: I guessed the bets in a mystery portfolio — {band}. {ending}
share.note: NO NUMBER, BY DESIGN. This level's portfolio is dealt from guessPool, the same pool level 7 draws from, so the same portfolio reaches other players; a card naming the answer would be a spoiler, and one naming the guess beside the band would be the answer worked out. The bands are this level's own star bands: 3 stars is stars.three.of, 2 stars is stars.two.of, and 1 star is everything else, since pass.measure is "guess" and this level cannot be failed. There is no "0" band for that reason. Each band carries its own ending: "Can you?" invites a friend to match a good result, and on the lowest band it would be inviting them to do worse, so that one asks them to get closer.

levels.revealLabel: Separate bets this portfolio really makes

levels.title: Three real bets
levels.challenge: Build a 5-holding portfolio that makes at least 3 separate bets.
levels.hint: Five names from under one heading is still close to one bet. Count the headings you have picked from, not the holdings, and try spreading the five across more of them.
levels.poolNote: The whole ticker list, all nine groups. Spreading across groups that really behave differently is the only way through this one.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: how many separate bets does your portfolio make?

levels.explain: Holdings from the same group tend to move together, so they collapse into one bet. Three real bets needs three groups that behave differently, not three names.
levels.why: Five AI stocks are nearly one bet. A fund, a bond fund, gold, an energy name and a staples name are closer to five, because what drives each of them differs.

share.headline: I found {value} bets in {holdings} holdings. Can you beat it?
share.note: docs/PRD.md's own example sentence. The portfolio is the player's own build off the whole ticker list, so the number gives nothing away to anybody else.

levels.revealLabel: Separate bets this portfolio really makes

levels.title: Hidden AI
levels.challenge: Keep at least 30% in QQQ, and still move less than half as much as the AI basket.
levels.hint: QQQ already carries a good deal of AI, so the other three need to move for reasons that have little to do with AI.
levels.holdingsNote: docs/PRD.md sets the 30% in QQQ and leaves the holding count open; 4 is chosen to match level 5 and to need no build rule the game does not already have. QQQ is dealt into the portfolio and cannot be removed, and its share cannot go below $3,000 of the $10,000.
levels.poolNote: The whole ticker list. QQQ is fixed; the other three are the level. What a player puts beside the fund is the only thing that can get the beta down.

basket.note: The 13 AI names frozen in basket.json, equally weighted and rebalanced daily, which is the same basket Hypothesis 2 measures and the same code that built it. basket.json is authoritative: a test holds this level to its 13 names.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: when the AI basket moves 1%, how far does your portfolio move?

pass.says: a beta to the AI basket under 0.50

levels.bucketNote: The edges are this level's own pass threshold (0.50) and the basket moving one for one (1.00), not new numbers. The lowest bucket has no floor because a beta has none: a portfolio of staples can move slightly against the basket, and that is still barely an AI bet.

share.headline: My portfolio moves {value}% for every 1% the AI basket moves. Can you get lower?
share.headlineBelowZero: My portfolio moves against the AI basket, not with it. Can you do the same?
share.note: A beta of 0.38 is 0.38% of movement per 1% of the basket's, which is why the headline carries the percent sign the reveal's number does not. bucketNote above records that a portfolio can move slightly AGAINST the basket; "moves -0.05% for every 1%" is a sentence a reader has to stop and decode, so a negative beta gets its own line.

levels.revealLabel: How far your portfolio moves with the AI basket
levels.explain: Beta says how far your portfolio moves when the AI basket moves: 1 means it moves with the basket one for one, 0 means the basket tells you nothing about it. QQQ holds the AI names near the top of the Nasdaq-100, so 30% of it already buys some of that exposure before you pick anything else. Buying AI stocks on top stacks the same bet twice.
levels.why: On the window this level was checked against, QQQ on its own had a beta of about 0.56 to the AI basket - more than this level allows. So the fund alone is already more than half an AI bet, and leaning harder on it is not the way out. What gets the beta under 0.50 is holding things the AI trade does not drive.

levels.title: Where's the risk?
levels.challenge: Build any 4-holding portfolio where no holding carries more than 35% of the risk.
levels.hint: Equal money isn't equal risk: the holding that swings hardest takes more than its quarter. Holdings that swing by similar amounts share the risk more evenly.
levels.poolNote: The whole ticker list, and any four of it, as docs/PRD.md asks.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: what share of your portfolio's risk does its biggest holding carry?

levels.guessNote: The floor is 25% by arithmetic: four shares adding to 100% put the biggest at a quarter or more. The ceiling is 100%, and a share can pass it when a holding offsets the rest, which no guess can name exactly - the three-star band still reaches it.

pass.says: no holding over 35% of the risk

levels.bucketNote: The edges are this level's own pass threshold (35%) and a half, not new numbers.

two.says: within 10 points of the real share

three.says: within 5 points of the real share

share.headline: No holding carries more than {value} of my risk. Can you spread it thinner?
share.note: True whether the level was passed or failed: maxRiskShare is the biggest share, so nothing carries more than it either way.

levels.revealLabel: Share of the risk in your biggest holding
levels.explain: Share of risk is not share of dollars. Each holding's share is its part of what makes the portfolio move, and the four shares add up to 100%, so they can be read straight against the money. A quarter of the money in the holding that swings hardest can be most of the risk.
levels.why: Spreading the risk evenly is not the same as making several bets. Four funds that all move together can each carry about a quarter of the risk and still be barely more than one bet, so a portfolio can pass this level and fail level 3. This level asks where the risk sits; level 3 asks how many different things it rides on.

levels.title: Crash test
levels.challenge: Build a 4-holding portfolio with at least 60% in stocks, then hold it through the February to March 2020 crash. Fall less than half as much as the S&P 500.
levels.hint: Sixty percent has to sit in stocks, so the question is which stocks. Through February and March 2020 the companies people kept paying for fell far less than the ones they stopped paying for.
levels.holdingsNote: docs/PRD.md sets the 60% in stocks and leaves the holding count open; 4 matches levels 4 and 5, and on real data it is the hardest of 3, 4 and 5 holdings while still having far more than the 3 winning designs the PRD asks for. The floor sits on a SET of holdings rather than on one, which is new: level 4's 30% sits on QQQ, and this level's 60% sits on whichever of the four holdings are stocks.
levels.poolNote: The whole ticker list. PLTR is shown disabled with its reason - it had not listed in February 2020 - rather than left out: a holding that vanishes explains nothing.

window.note: 19 February to 23 March 2020, 24 trading days - the closes, as docs/PRD.md's crash table counts them, with 23 daily moves between them - bought and held and never rebalanced, against VOO's adjusted closes labelled 'S&P 500 (VOO, with dividends)'. Every one of those is fixed in docs/PRD.md and read from data/crashes.json, not decided here. This level's prices are history and never move, so unlike levels 1 to 5 its answer is the same every week - the window block above, and its 252-day minimum, do not apply to it.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: for every 1% the S&P 500 fell, how much did your portfolio fall?

levels.guessNote: 1.00 - falling with the index, one for one - sits exactly in the middle of the slider, so the left half is 'held up better than the market' and the right half is 'fell harder'. The range does not cover every build: across the legal 4-holding builds the real answer runs from -0.117, a portfolio that ROSE 3.96% while the index fell, to 1.714, almost all of it in COP. Both ends are corners a player reaches only by pushing one holding as far as the $100 steps allow, and at both the bucket star still lands; it is the within-0.10 star that cannot be reached there. Level 5 makes the same trade for the same reason.

pass.says: a fall under half the S&P 500's

buckets.label: held up - less than half the index's fall

levels.bucketNote: The edges are this level's own pass threshold (0.50) and the portfolio falling one for one with the index (1.00) - the same 'one for one' edge level 4 uses for the AI basket, and here it is the index itself: all of VOO gives exactly 1.000 in this window. The lowest bucket has no floor because the answer goes below zero when a portfolio rises while the index falls, which this window allows.

share.headline: My portfolio fell {value} times as far as the S&P 500 in the 2020 crash. Can you fall less?
share.headlineAtOrBelowZero: My portfolio did not fall at all while the S&P 500 fell in the 2020 crash. Can you?
share.note: "Times as far" is how this level's own explain reads the number: "0.50 means you fell half as far". guessNote above records that a legal build reaches -0.117 - a portfolio that ROSE while the index fell - and "fell -0.12 times as far" is not clumsy but false, so zero and below get their own line.

levels.revealLabel: How much of the index's fall your portfolio took
levels.explain: This level asks a different question from the others: not how many bets you made, but what happened when everything fell at once. The S&P 500 fell 33.99% in five weeks. Your answer is your own fall as a share of that one: 0.50 means you fell half as far, 1.00 means you fell with it, and above 1.00 means you fell harder. The 60% in stocks is there so the answer cannot be bought by simply holding less of the market.
levels.why: What cushioned this crash was long government bonds: TLT rose 14.23% while the index lost 33.99%, and most of the portfolios that pass hold something like it. That is this crash, not a rule about bonds. In the 2022 bear market TLT fell 29.33%, MORE than the S&P 500's own 24.52% - rates rose, and bonds fell alongside shares instead of cushioning them. You can watch that happen in Crash replay's 2022 window. So the lesson is not 'hold bonds': it is that what protects a portfolio depends on what the crash is made of, and you cannot know that in advance.
levels.crashNote: Both TLT numbers are read from data/crashes.json, bought and held over each window's own dates, the same way the level measures a portfolio.

levels.title: One trade
levels.challenge: Three mystery portfolios, one after another. Guess how many separate bets each one makes. Every guess has to land within 1.
levels.hint: Holdings under one heading count as roughly one bet, and even different headings of stocks partly move together, so the answer is usually well below the number of holdings.

series.note: Three portfolios in one level, each guessed and revealed in turn before the next appears. The order is fixed and the first portfolio is always the registered one: see BUILD_LOG.md, session 2.10, for why that matters to Hypothesis 3.

parts.note: The registered draw. PREREG.md's Hypothesis 3: level 2's portfolio and this one are both drawn from the pool of 20, so on average they are equally hard. Every pool portfolio this browser has already seen is excluded, so a player is never asked the same portfolio twice - that would measure memory, not learning. The marginal draw is still uniform over all 20.
One of the two strata, which one decided by the same draw that fills part 3 with the other. PREREG.md does not reach this portfolio.
Whichever stratum part 2 did not take. The gap between the two bands is above 2 bets, so no single number is within 1 of both and the level cannot be passed without reading the portfolios.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: how many separate bets does this portfolio make?
guess.rangeNote: 1 to 6, the same slider level 2 uses. The top covers the capstone pool's highest answer plus 1, so a player can always land within 1 of it.

two.says: two of your three guesses within half a bet

three.says: all three within half a bet

levels.explain: This is every level at once. A portfolio can hold eight things and make one bet, or hold six and make four: what decides it is whether the holdings move together, not how many there are or how the money is split. Guessing three in a row is the test of that, because one number cannot be right about all three.
levels.why: The first of these three portfolios comes from the same pool of 20 that dealt your level 2 portfolio, so the two are equally hard on average - that pair of guesses is how Hypothesis 3 measures whether players improve. It is never the same portfolio you saw on level 2.

share.headline: Three mystery portfolios — {band}. {ending}

bands.2: two of three within half a bet
bands.3: all three within half a bet

share.note: The same spoiler rule as level 2, for the same reason: part 1 is drawn from guessPool and parts 2 and 3 from finalPool, and all three reach other players. Each band is the rule js/levels.js's seriesVerdict() applies for that many stars: 3 is all three inside stars.three.of, 2 is exactly two inside it (three would be 3 stars), 1 is the pass rule alone - all three within pass.of - and 0 is failing that. The 0-star ending asks for all three rather than saying "Can you?", which on a failed card would be inviting a friend to miss too.

levels.revealLabel: Separate bets this portfolio really makes

dailyPuzzle.note: The daily 'Same bet?' puzzle, docs/PRD.md Feature roadmap Tier 1. Five ticker pairs a day, the same for every player, answered as one of three buckets. Every rule the builder applies is here rather than in code, so an instructor or a reviewer can read what makes a day's puzzle without reading scripts/build_puzzles.mjs.
dailyPuzzle.daysNote: About one year of daily returns, and deliberately NOT the 756-day window the levels use. docs/PRD.md says the puzzle is 'scored on last year's correlation'. The two windows disagree, and visibly: VTI and VXUS correlate 0.7997 over 756 days and 0.8655 over 252, so the same pair is a near miss on level 1 and the same bet in the puzzle. Every reveal therefore names its own window.
dailyPuzzle.bucketsNote: The three buckets are level 1's own, read from this file at build time and never re-typed here: 0.7 and above is the same bet, 0.3 to 0.7 is partly, below 0.3 is different bets. One definition, so the two screens cannot drift apart.
dailyPuzzle.guardBandNote: A pair whose correlation sits within 0.05 of a bucket edge is never used. The puzzle scores a bucket with no slider and no partial credit, so a pair at 0.7099 would be a coin flip rather than a question. On the window measured on 25 November 2026 this drops 84 of the 780 pairs.
dailyPuzzle.singleSlotNote: Each day holds all three answers, two of one, two of another and one of the third. These weights choose which answer gets the single slot: 'the same bet' on 5 days in 7. It is weighted because the pools are nothing like equal - 24 pairs correlate above 0.7 against 507 below 0.3 - so an even split would show the same handful of same-bet pairs every eight days. At these weights the gap between two showings of one same-bet pair is 15 days at its shortest and 19 on average.
dailyPuzzle.maxPerAnswerNote: No answer is correct more than twice in a day, so always picking one answer cannot score 3 of 5. Measured over 60 days: always 'different bets' scores 1.85, always 'partly' 1.90, always 'the same bet' 1.25.
dailyPuzzle.maxPerTickerNote: No ticker appears in more than two of a day's five pairs, so one name cannot carry the whole day.
dailyPuzzle.relaxationsNote: A pair used in the last 14 days is not used again. If that leaves a bucket unable to fill its slots, the window halves to 7 and then to 0, in this fixed order, and the entry records which one it used; the three-answer mix and the surprise are never dropped, and a day that cannot be built fails the build rather than shipping a weaker puzzle. A LONGER window is not better: at 18 days the 24-pair same-bet pool cannot fill it, the fallback fires, and the shortest gap gets worse, not better - 12 days against 15.

kinds.label: the same bet, from different groups
kinds.line: Different groups, same bet: these two moved together over the last year.

kinds.label: different bets, from the same group
kinds.line: Same group, different bets: these two moved mostly independently over the last year.

surprise.lineNote: The sentence the screen shows when a pair is a surprise. Written here rather than in js/dailyView.js because it is a claim about what the prices did, and it is tied to the window the puzzle measures - the last year - rather than stated as something permanent. Correlations change; a sentence that says they do not would be wrong by next year.
surprise.note: At least one pair a day where the answer disagrees with the group the two tickers sit in, which is the lesson the game is named after. Groups come from tickers.json. The day's seed chooses which kind, among the kinds that still have an unused pair. Kind A is scarce - all 10 of its pairs are also same-bet pairs - so it leads about a third of days and appears on about half.

dailyPuzzle.orderNote: The surprise is the fifth pair, so a day ends on the pair that teaches most.
dailyPuzzle.horizonNote: Each build writes any missing entry from tomorrow through tomorrow + 6, which carries the puzzle across weekends, market holidays and a run of failed fetches. A build may rewrite an entry dated after its own New York date and may never touch one dated on or before it: that date is being played, or has been.
dailyPuzzle.timeZoneNote: The puzzle turns over with the market, so two devices in different time zones get the same five pairs.

weekly.note: The weekly challenge: one mystery portfolio a week, the same one for everybody, changing at midnight New York time on Monday. docs/PRD.md, milestone 2 step 8: "one new mystery portfolio each Monday, so there's a reason to come back and to post about it." It is not one of the seven levels and has no place in the ladder; it borrows their shape so that js/round.js, the "Why?" cards and the share card work on it unchanged.
weekly.modeNote: What a round of this reports about itself, so a "Why?" card written for the weekly can lead on it and stay silent on the levels. See js/why.js's LEAD_MATCHES.
weekly.title: Weekly challenge
weekly.challenge: One mystery portfolio a week. Guess how many separate bets it makes.
weekly.firstMondayNote: The first week. Before this date the screen says when the challenge starts rather than dealing a portfolio from before it existed, and the cycle counts weeks from here, so two browsers on the same date agree without storing anything or asking anybody.
weekly.cyclesNote: Ten portfolios, and week 11 is week 1 again. A player who has seen them all has seen them all; cycling is better than running out, and the answers move with the prices anyway.

window.anchorNote: EVERY PLAYER IN A WEEK GETS THE SAME ANSWER, so the window ends on the Friday before the Monday rather than on the latest day in data/game.json, which changes every weekday evening. If that Friday was a holiday the anchor walks back to the last day the file carries, which needs no holiday calendar. The file keeps the most recent 756 days, so early in a week the anchored window is a few days shorter than 756; across the ten portfolios that moves an answer by at most 0.022 bets, which cannot change a star and is checked by tests/weekly.test.js.

guess.prompt: Before the reveal: how many separate bets does this portfolio make?
guess.rangeNote: 1 to 6, the slider levels 2 and 7 use. The ten answers all sit inside it, which tests/weekly.test.js checks against the live data: an answer above the top could not be guessed within 1 by anybody.

share.hidesAnswerNote: EVERYBODY HAS THE SAME PORTFOLIO THIS WEEK, which makes a card naming the answer a spoiler for every player who has not gone yet - a wider leak than levels 2 and 7, where only the one player in twenty who draws the same portfolio could use it. So the card carries the stars and how close the guess came, and neither the answer nor the guess. The portfolio's NAME is not on it either: "Gold, bonds, oil and staples" is a list of the holdings in words.
share.headline: This week’s mystery portfolio — {band}. {ending}

weekly.explain: Effective bets counts independent sources of risk, not holdings. Holdings that move together collapse into one bet, and a quiet holding can take a big share of the money while adding little to the count - because the count measures risk, not money.
weekly.why: A new portfolio every Monday, the same one for every player, measured over the three years ending the Friday before. Nothing about your guess leaves the browser.
weekly.revealLabel: Separate bets this portfolio really makes
weekly.portfoliosNote: Ten hand-built portfolios, each a lesson. None of them holds the same set of tickers as any of the 40 in guessPool or finalPool - those belong to Hypothesis 3, and a portfolio a player already met on level 2 is not a mystery. The answers are spread so that one number typed every week earns 3 stars on at most 3 of the 10: no four of them sit within a bet of each other. Both rules are checked against the live data by tests/weekly.test.js, not against numbers written down here, so a market that moves the answers together turns the run red instead of quietly making the challenge guessable. The bets below are what the committed data/game.json gave on 26 November 2026 and are a comment, never read by the game.

portfolios.name: One from every group
portfolios.lesson: Eight holdings, eight groups, and fewer than three bets. Spreading the names is not spreading the risk.

portfolios.name: The barbell
portfolios.lesson: Half the money in the quietest thing on the list, and it still makes barely more than one bet.

portfolios.name: Four that go their own ways
portfolios.lesson: Four holdings, more bets than the eight above: what matters is whether they move together.

portfolios.name: Five groups, one bet
portfolios.lesson: Five holdings in five different groups, no holding carrying more than a quarter of the risk - and still barely more than one bet. Spreading the money is not spreading the risk.
portfolios.replacesNote: It replaced a two-holding portfolio (KO and TLT) that no rule could explain, so its reveal showed the fallback card. A rule for it would have fired on one portfolio in the whole game: of the 62 the game deals or writes down, four hold exactly two things, and the other three already have cards. See BUILD_LOG.md, session 2.18.

portfolios.name: A tech fund and four quiet things
portfolios.lesson: The loud holding takes most of the risk, and the quiet ones still buy real bets.

portfolios.name: Three that share no customers
portfolios.lesson: Three holdings in three different businesses, and still not three bets.

portfolios.name: Five, none of them alike
portfolios.lesson: Metal, oil, health, staples and one giant: about as far apart as five holdings get here.

portfolios.name: Oil, drugs and software
portfolios.lesson: Three industries that do not rise and fall together.

portfolios.name: Quiet money, one loud corner
portfolios.lesson: Most of the money in the calmest holdings and a little in the wildest: the most bets this list can make.

weekly.orderNote: THE ORDER IS THE POINT, not just the set. Sorted by answer the ten rise from 1.11 to 4.40, and a player who came back every week could guess "a bit more than last week" without reading the portfolio. Here no two weeks in a row are within a bet of each other, INCLUDING the wrap from week 10 back to week 1, since the list cycles - the tightest step is 1.28. Found by searching every ordering for the one whose tightest step is widest, then rotating the cycle to open on five famous companies that turn out to be one trade, which is the lesson the game is named for. tests/weekly.test.js checks the rule against the live prices.

guessPool.note: Level 2's portfolio and the first of level 7's mystery portfolios are both drawn from this one pool, as PREREG.md requires, so on average they are equally hard.
guessPool.seedNote: A game seed, deliberately not the registered seed 2026.
guessPool.expectedBetsNote: Computed from the committed data/prices.json when the pool was generated. The game recomputes it at play time; a test holds the two to 1e-9.

displayNote: guess.step, guess.display and revealLabel are presentation, and they are data here rather than a branch in js/game.js: with five levels answering with a correlation, a bets count, a beta and a share of risk, code that switched on the measure name would decide how a number reads. A display of "percent" means the value is a share of 1 and is shown as a whole percent, or to 2 decimal places when it sits within 0.005 of the level's threshold.

finalPool.note: Level 7's second and third mystery portfolios, one drawn from each stratum. PREREG.md does not reach this pool: Hypothesis 3 covers only the FIRST mystery portfolio, which comes from guessPool. See BUILD_LOG.md, session 2.10.
finalPool.seedNote: A game seed, and deliberately neither 2026 nor the pool of 20's seed.
finalPool.topWeightCapNote: The biggest holding carries at most this share of the money. Effective bets rises when money is pushed into one holding with the holdings unchanged, so without this cap a portfolio could earn a high answer through concentration - and a player applying the game's own lesson about spreading risk would be marked wrong for it.
finalPool.strataNote: Portfolio 2 is drawn from one stratum and portfolio 3 from the other. The gap between the bands is above 2 bets, so no single number is within 1 of both and the capstone cannot be passed without reading the portfolios.
finalPool.expectedBetsNote: Computed from the committed data/prices.json when the pool was generated. The game recomputes it at play time; a test holds the two to 1e-9.

portfolios.handPlacedReason: docs/PRD.md's own example - an S&P 500 fund, a tech fund and NVIDIA - which is the sentence the game is named after. Placed by hand because 8,000 candidate draws never built it and no pool-of-20 portfolio is this trio, so a drawn pool would almost certainly never show a player the case the game is named for.
